title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measure whether adding a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier plus a bounded automated repair step increases the fraction of intent‑driven network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. Each pair reused a single shared_initial LLM candidate and compared: (a) baseline — accept the single candidate, and (b) guarded — run deterministic validation and permit ≤1 automated repair. Results: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and the restricted repair budget, single‑shot generation was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue. We release preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts and interpret results with respect to estimand conditioning, validator coverage, repair budget, and operational policies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are rapidly being adopted to help automate NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and configuration repair. For pre‑deployment network changes, semantic correctness properties—ordering/sequence constraints, reachability, and policy preservation—are operationally decisive and cannot be judged by surface syntactic checks alone. A widespread engineering pattern is generate→validate→repair: combine a generative model with deterministic validators and bounded automated repair to reduce operational risk. However, the measurable benefit of such guarded pipelines depends on the experimental estimand (what is held fixed), the single‑shot quality of the generator, the validator's expressiveness, and the permitted repair budget.

We preregistered and executed a paired experiment that isolates deterministic rescue available when the same single LLM draw (shared_initial) is evaluated under two treatments: (1) baseline — accept the single candidate, and (2) guarded — run a deterministic validator and allow at most one constrained automated repair. Our primary research question: does adding a deterministic verifier plus at most one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting that same candidate without repair? The study is intended to bound the rescue available under operational policies that restrict model calls per change request.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and system papers document a diverse set of LLM applications to NetOps (intent translation, template synthesis, protocol test generation, repair) and emphasize tool‑augmentation patterns that enable external validator or planner calls to improve end‑to‑end correctness [1–4]. Planner‑centric and ReAct‑style tool‑use frameworks allow LLMs to orchestrate multiple deterministic tools and have been proposed to manage multi‑step NetOps workflows [2,5]. Empirical reports indicate that generate→validate→repair scaffolds can improve correctness metrics compared with unconstrained generation, but absolute gains depend on validator coverage and whether pipelines permit resampling or iterative regeneration [3,4]. Work on hallucination detection and deterministic safety nets offers complementary detection and mitigation approaches (entropy/consistency detectors, retrieval augmentation, self‑reflection), but effectiveness is task‑dependent [6]. Prior hybrid repair studies combining symbolic fault localization with generative repair operators report variable success that depends strongly on the verifier's semantic reach and the permitted edit operator set [7,8].

Two methodological themes motivated our design. First, many prior evaluations conflate verifier benefits with benefits from multiple independent model draws or verifier‑guided regeneration; this conflation obscures the deterministic post‑hoc rescue attributable to a fixed model draw. Second, available NetOps benchmarks often emphasize syntactic/template correctness rather than semantically rich invariants (sequencing, reachability, policy preservation), limiting operational generality. We therefore preregistered a paired design conditioned on a single shared_initial draw and a constrained repair budget to isolate deterministic rescue under tight model‑call budgets.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The confirmatory design was preregistered under study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001. The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) on N = 300 paired intents after applying preregistered inclusion/exclusion rules. The preregistration and analysis executor were frozen prior to the main run.

Task generation and stratification. The task suite is a deterministic synthetic topology and intent generator stratified into three difficulty levels (low/medium/high). Each task manifest encodes (i) the natural‑language intent, (ii) initial and expected final device states, (iii) required sequencing constraints, (iv) preservation invariants, and (v) protected interfaces. The confirmatory main run sampled 100 pairs per stratum.

Shared_initial protocol, model, validator, and repair operator. To measure only deterministic rescue we used the shared_initial estimand: for each pair a single LLM candidate (shared_initial) was produced and reused verbatim for both conditions. The declared generator was gpt-5-mini (execution configuration records requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"). Semantic evaluation employed a deterministic validator implementing full intent‑constraint checks (sequencing, required_command_count, preservation of unspecified state, topology reachability rules, and forbidden‑template protections). The guarded pipeline permitted at most one automated repair (repair budget ≤ 1). The repair operator is a constrained localized edit routine limited to sequencing/insertion edits (e.g., inserting a missing 'admin down' prior to a VLAN/MTU change); repairs were only attempted when the validator flagged the shared_initial candidate. Repair attempts were revalidated deterministically.

Contamination controls, exclusions, and analysis plan. The preregistration included negative controls and deterministic contamination checks. A pair would be excluded from confirmatory analysis only if both pipeline calls failed due to provider/infrastructure outage. The primary confirmatory test is a paired exact McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant counts (n10,n01), accompanied by a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Secondary analyses and stratum tests were prespecified as exploratory and multiplicity‑controlled where reported.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and integrity. The adapter completed the confirmatory run with 600 episodes (300 pairs). Provider audit shows a total of 301 hosted model calls consistent with the shared_initial protocol plus one repair invocation (model_calls_used = 301; repair_stage_count = 1). No pairs were excluded under the preregistered rules and deterministic reconciliation confirmed consistent episode accounting.

Primary outcomes. Binary scoring produced baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300: baseline = 299/300 = 0.9966667 and guarded = 300/300 = 1.0. The paired contingency table is n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed absolute paired improvement (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333. The exact two‑sided McNemar test on the discordant pairs yields p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729, B = 10000) for the absolute paired difference is [0.00, 0.01]. Because discordance is minimal (m = n10 + n01 = 1), the exact test has limited sensitivity; the bootstrap CI bounds the plausible absolute improvement to at most one percentage point given the current estimand and suite.

Per‑stratum diagnostics and repair trace. Per stratum: low difficulty baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; medium baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; high baseline = 99/100 and guarded = 100/100. The single discordant episode occurred in the high stratum. Validator traces attribute the initial failure to a sequencing omission (a required 'admin down' was missing). The constrained repair operator applied one localized insertion and the validator then reported a pass; this repair produced the deterministic rescue recorded in the guarded condition. The marginal model‑call cost for that rescue was one additional repair invocation across 300 pairs.

Contamination and missingness. Contamination checks and negative controls did not raise anomalies in the main run. There were zero failed or unscorable episodes and no excluded pairs under the preregistered missingness rules.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation under estimand conditioning. The shared_initial estimand reflects operational policies that tightly limit model calls: it isolates deterministic rescue afforded by post‑hoc checking and a bounded repair budget applied to a fixed candidate. In this experimental context single‑shot generation was near ceiling; consequently the guarded pipeline produced only one deterministic rescue and the observed absolute benefit was small. This outcome emphasizes that the measurable advantage of a guarded pipeline depends on the baseline single‑shot quality of the generator, the distribution of failure modes in the deployment domain, and the validator's semantic reach.

Ceiling effects and power considerations. The preregistration targeted detection of larger absolute improvements; however, without executing the optional calibration pilot to estimate discordance, the main run confronted near‑ceiling baseline performance (299/300) and thus limited statistical power to detect small absolute differences. Small calibration pilots can be useful when generator performance on a chosen suite may approach ceiling.

Validator scope and failure‑mode dependence. The single observed failure mode was a sequencing omission; other failure classes (reachability violations, forbidden‑ACL alterations) were not observed at scale in the synthetic suite. The guarded pipeline's practical value in other deployments will depend on (a) the prevalence of validator‑detectable failure modes and (b) the validator's expressiveness. Richer validators (e.g., full reachability analysis) or broader repair operators could increase rescue rates but change the estimand and operational cost profile.

Repair budget, cost, and operational tradeoffs. We intentionally limited repair to a single constrained edit to bound deterministic rescue under minimal extra model calls. Empirically, the guarded rescue required one extra invocation in 300 pairs (model_calls_used = 301), so bounded repair imposed negligible marginal model‑call cost in this run. Organizations should align pipeline design, permitted repair operations, and model‑call budgets with their operational risk tolerance and governance constraints.

Relation to prior work. Our design complements tool‑augmented evaluations that permit resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration by providing an artifact‑grounded bound on deterministic rescue when only a single LLM draw is allowed. Where prior studies report larger gains, those gains often combine deterministic checks with additional model draws or interactive steering; such workflows correspond to different estimands and operational tradeoffs [2–4,7].
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study conditioning on a single shared_initial LLM draw, a deterministic validator plus a ≤1 automated repair budget produced one deterministic rescue among 300 synthetic NetOps intents (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300; absolute paired improvement = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00,0.01]). Under the evaluated synthetic suite and repair design, single‑shot generation was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue. These results provide an operationally meaningful bound on deterministic verifier/repair benefit under tight model‑call budgets and illustrate how estimand conditioning, validator coverage, and repair policy determine observed gains. We archive the preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and targeted follow‑ups that vary estimand conditioning, task distributions, model strength, or repair budgets for broader operational evaluation.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated deterministically; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase validator marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative generation).
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
